sources.title: Happy: How Happy fits together; Original Happy CLI
sources.locator: How Happy fits together; Original Happy CLI
sources.finding: Happy provides Desktop for macOS, Windows and Linux; mobile iOS, Android and web; and its original happy CLI wrapping Claude Code or Codex. Desktop uses a separate Happy Agent runtime for multi-model sessions and teams.

sources.title: Happy: Mobile access
sources.finding: Paired phone apps continue the same encrypted sessions and allow users to read work and respond away from the desktop.

sources.title: Happy: Supported providers; Switch models
sources.finding: Happy runs Claude, Codex and Grok on the user's existing Claude Code, Codex or Grok CLI sign-ins, Gemini through Antigravity, and OpenCode or other ACP agents on their own login (beta). Model or effort can change mid-session without discarding the transcript.

sources.title: Happy: Models and Subscriptions
sources.finding: Happy uses existing Claude Code, Codex and Grok CLI sign-ins, so no Happy plan or pasted key is needed for model access; Antigravity and ACP agents use their own login. Bedrock works with an API key or the AWS credential chain.

sources.title: Happy: Add a project
sources.finding: Importing registers an existing folder without moving, copying or initializing Git. A project without Git uses a plain folder copy when a workspace is needed.

sources.title: Happy: REST API
sources.finding: Happy Agent exposes a token-authenticated REST API for sessions, streaming events and control on user infrastructure. The original happy CLI is a separate product-owned terminal entry point.

sources.title: Happy: Skills and MCP
sources.finding: Skills are SKILL.md files and MCP servers are mcp.toml entries, shared by every model; an agent can write both. MCP tools need Auto or Full access and every Auto call is reviewed. MCP servers from Codex or Claude Code configuration are not imported.

sources.title: Happy: Chief of Staff
sources.finding: The built-in Chief of Staff handles setup and task creation through ordinary conversation, including projects, remote hosts and teams. Persistent standalone issue metadata is not established.

sources.title: Happy: Subagents
sources.finding: Subagent trees are capped at depth three and at most five agents including finished children. Sessions have exact agent IDs for messaging and retained follow-up. This is session hierarchy, not verified issue dependency enforcement.

sources.title: Happy: Add a project
sources.finding: AGENTS.md files in the project tree are read by each agent and reread when they change; global AGENTS.md applies across projects.

sources.title: Happy: Subagents; What Happy Desktop shows
sources.finding: Subagents run in the background by default and return completion to the parent. Desktop displays subagents and running tools; tree size is bounded.

sources.title: Happy: How agents work in another workspace
sources.locator: How agents work in another workspace
sources.finding: Bots and their subtasks may create a full conversation in a new workspace, with the creator as coordinator. Only the creating session may archive that workspace.

sources.title: Happy: Subagents; How agents message each other
sources.locator: Subagents; How agents message each other
sources.finding: Agents delegate bounded work, choose each child model and effort, receive background completion notices and send follow-ups to finished children with retained context. Exact IDs route messages across projects or machines.

sources.title: Happy: Durable waits and scheduled messages
sources.finding: Primary sessions can schedule messages to known agent IDs, list or cancel them and survive intervening runtime restarts. Durable waits end early on new input. This establishes scheduled work, not an unrestricted external-event scheduler.

sources.title: Happy: Inbox and presence
sources.finding: Agent questions remain in the conversation and experimental Inbox; answering on one device closes the shared state. Away presence instructs agents to continue with notes instead of waiting indefinitely.

sources.title: Happy: What Happy Desktop shows
sources.finding: Per-session UI shows phase, tools, background processes, subagents, waiting state, whole-tree token usage and changed files. Fleet navigation has not been measured.

sources.title: Happy: What you get
sources.finding: The built-in Chief of Staff configures accounts, imports projects, pairs phones, deploys remote agents and creates teams through conversation.

sources.title: Happy: Remote server
sources.finding: Happy Agent can run on an always-on user server while Desktop connects over Tailcat and phones connect through an encrypted relay. Closing the controlling laptop does not stop work on that reachable host. Users supply host compute.

sources.title: Happy: How Happy creates a workspace
sources.finding: Parallel workspaces use Git worktrees on branches cut from the remote trunk. File sync and setup commands run per workspace; nongit projects use a plain copy.

sources.title: Happy: What the OS sandbox enforces
sources.finding: The documented OS sandbox uses macOS Seatbelt or Linux namespaces and seccomp. Shell writes, network and host sockets are restricted; file tools can still read credential folders, and MCP servers run outside the sandbox. Docker-backed sessions nest that sandbox inside the container.

sources.title: Happy: Agents That Never Die
sources.finding: Conversations and child sessions persist across window closure and runtime restart; finished children accept follow-ups with their full context. This is a documentation claim, not a crash test.

sources.title: Happy: How Happy creates a workspace
sources.finding: New workspaces copy configured sync files and run setup_commands. They start with a cold build cache. A failed setup command logs a warning while checkout and file sync determine readiness.

sources.title: Happy: Use several accounts; Provider usage and quotas
sources.locator: Use several accounts; Provider usage and quotas
sources.finding: Smart provider pools can rotate same-provider accounts after authentication or quota-exhaustion errors. Provider quotas are polled about every fifteen minutes and are observations rather than billing records.

sources.title: Happy: What Happy Desktop shows
sources.finding: Session status includes active tools, background work, subagents, waiting state, tokens and changed files. Deliberate failure and approval consistency after reconnect remain untested.

sources.title: Happy: Provider usage and quotas
sources.finding: Provider quotas are polled about every fifteen minutes and shown in the app; they are observations, not billing records.

sources.title: Happy: Shared work
sources.finding: Team members see the same projects and sessions and can speak to the agent. Changes in speaker include the member name/email; per-member drafts and task ordering stay personal.

sources.title: Happy: Owner; Sign-in; Leaving
sources.finding: Team mode verifies per-user WorkOS tokens. The owner alone renames the installation, toggles global skills or archives others tasks; members otherwise have equal access and can select Full access. A remove-member action is explicitly not built yet.

sources.title: Happy: Four permission modes; Auto review
sources.finding: Read only, Workspace write, Auto and Full access share a permission model. Auto sends boundary-crossing actions to a separate read-only reviewer and grants only that execution if allowed. Reads and workspace edits are not reviewed.

sources.title: Happy: Switch models; How compaction works
sources.finding: Session transcripts retain provider-specific opaque data; compaction creates a visible message describing replaced content. No immutable audit retention guarantee was verified.

sources.title: Happy: Initial core release; Current interface
